blocks.content: kubectl apply is the declarative way to create or update an object from a manifest, safe to run repeatedly, and the standard command behind real, ongoing Kubernetes workflows.
1. Declarative: Create or Update, Whichever Fits
blocks.text: 1. Declarative: Create or Update, Whichever Fits

blocks.content: apply looks at a manifest and figures out what to do, creating the object if it does not exist yet, or updating it to match if it does, you describe the end state, apply handles getting there.

blocks.alt: One command, whichever action, create or update, actually applies

blocks.content: -f points apply at the YAML file describing what should exist, exactly the manifests covered throughout this course, from Pods to Deployments to Services.

blocks.alt: A manifest file describing the desired end state

blocks.content: This is a genuinely important property, running apply against the exact same, unchanged manifest twice in a row produces the exact same result both times, no error, no duplicate object, this idempotence is what makes it safe to use in automated pipelines.

blocks.alt: The same result, every time, whether run once or repeatedly

blocks.content: This is exactly why apply, not create (covered in the next topic), is the standard for real, ongoing workflows, create is a one-time, imperative action that fails if the object already exists, apply handles both cases gracefully.

blocks.alt: Declarative and repeatable versus imperative and one-time only

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl apply -f is declarative, creating an object if it is missing or updating it to match if it already exists, safe to run repeatedly.
This idempotence is exactly why apply, not create, is the standard command for real, ongoing, automated Kubernetes workflows.
